NFIRS holiday-season fire analysis

Scope: all departments (national). Years: 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024. Generated 2026-10-21 14:29. Primary incidents only (EXP_NO = 0); exposure fires excluded. Aid-given records (AID 3, 4, 5) excluded to avoid double counting. Residential = PROP_USE 400–499; structure fire = INC_TYPE 110–118, 120–123.

Summary

H1 — Thanksgiving the top day for residential structure fires: Thanksgiving was the #1 day of Nov–Dec in 4 of 5 years and the #1 day of the whole year in 4 of 5. On average Thanksgiving had 1.98× the typical Nov–Dec day (median rank 1 of 61).
Split by fire type: for confined cooking fires Thanksgiving averaged 3.56× a typical Nov–Dec day; for non-confined (the larger, more damaging fires) it averaged 1.07× (median rank 19). This shows how much of any Thanksgiving peak is driven by small kitchen fires.
H2 — Holiday season elevated: residential structure fires per day were higher in Nov–Dec than Jan–Oct in 5 of 5 years. Busiest month by year: Jan (2×), Feb (1×), Dec (1×), Nov (1×). If January/February rival or beat Nov–Dec, the pattern is a winter (heating) effect rather than a holiday effect — compare the 'excl. holidays' column.
For all fires (including outdoor, vehicle, brush), Nov–Dec was higher than Jan–Oct in 0 of 5 years.

Claim check — the “17 million holiday fires” survey statistic

The claim: nearly 17 million Americans (7%) report having personally experienced a home fire during the holiday season; cooking/baking caused 31%, and 29% involved electrical wiring, outlets or rechargeable-battery appliances. NFIRS figures below are residential structure fires, Nov 1 – Dec 31, seasons 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024.

Cooking: NFIRS shows cooking as the cause of 39.2% of Nov–Dec residential structure fires (48.4% of those with a known cause). The survey's 31% is 8 points below what fire departments record.
Electrical / battery devices: even the most generous NFIRS grouping — electrical malfunction + appliances + equipment failure — accounts for 9.8% of fires (12.1% of those with a known cause), against the survey's 29%. NFIRS has no battery-specific cause code, so battery fires fall within these categories. The survey's 29% is 19 points above what fire departments record.
Scale: fire departments reported 35,515–45,941 residential structure fires per Nov–Dec season to NFIRS (average 40,199; about 263 civilian deaths per season). 17 million people is about 6.8 million households at 2.5 people each — about 169× the reported fires in one season. The survey figure can only be reconciled as lifetime recall that counts small fires never reported to a fire department; it does not describe how many holiday fires happen in a year. Ask for the exact question wording, timeframe, definition of “fire”, sample and sponsor.

NFIRS participation is voluntary and not every department reports, so NFIRS undercounts fire-department responses; it also never captures fires handled without calling the fire department. The cause shares are less affected than the totals.

What rises in Nov–Dec? (seasonal lift, pooled across years)

Lift = average per day in Nov–Dec ÷ average per day Jan–Oct. 1.5 means 50% more per day during the holidays. Rare codes are filtered out. 'Extra incidents' is the count above what the Jan–Oct pace would predict.
